CapEx (capital expenditure) heavy projects take a lot of time and planning, and look like a big bump in the road to get over; any failing at any step can ruin it and cost the entire expenditure for nothing. OpEx (operational expenditure) projects are smoother from the budget standpoint and are easier for smoothbrained managers (who have been promoted beyond their competency) to handle.

Take for example IT. You could spend a few hundred K and provision a small server room with enough gear to last the company for five years with minimal ongoing opex and plenty of potential for lower cost upgrades or expansions in the future. However, you have to do all that work up front and not fuck it up. Or, you could rent cloud servers and spend more over the next 3 years than you would in total with running your own, but you don’t have to know as much, it costs very little up front, and you don’t assume anywhere near as much risk.

If you’re the brass and you know your staff are midwits, you’ll probably want to do the latter because it’s more flexible and harder to fuck up. The additional monthly cost adds up to more over time but is easier to budget for month to month, and so it’s an attractive prospect.

This is an English locational surname. It derives from one of the villages called Dunham in the county of Nottingham, or Dunham Magna and Dunham Parva, in Norfolk, or Dunham on the Hill, in both Norfolk and Cheshire. The origin is the pre 7th century Olde English "dun" meaning a hill and "ham," a hamlet or homstead. In effect the villages called Dunham on the Hill are repeating themselves, as Dunham means on the hill! Locational surnames were usually given to people after they left their original homes and moved elsewhere. It was in medieval times, and to some extent remains so to-day, that one of the easiest ways to identify a stranger was to call him, or sometimes her, by the name of the place from whence they came. This often lead to mispellings of the surname as applies in this case in that the surname is found as Dunham and Donham or sometimes even Doneham. Early examples of the surname recording include those of Edwarde Dunham at the village of North Elmham in Norfolk, on October 9th 1546, during the reign of King Henry V111 (!510 - 1547), and in Cheshire that of Thomas Donham, a witness at the town of Nantwich on November 5th 1790.
